Uchinoura Space Center, 2003-05-09. JAXA's first-of-its-kind sample-return mission to a near-Earth asteroid. Hayabusa (Japanese for 'falcon') carried four μ10 microwave-discharge ion thrusters — the first microwave-discharge ion engines ever flown.
M-V-5 fourth stage delivers Hayabusa onto a heliocentric trajectory toward asteroid Itokawa.
2004-05-19. Earth swingby provides the orbital energy needed to reach Itokawa's higher-eccentricity orbit.

2005-09-12. Hayabusa arrived at 25143 Itokawa — a 540×270×210-m near-Earth asteroid. The body is too small to orbit gravitationally; the spacecraft station-kept at a 20-km gate position and descended for sample attempts.

Two touchdowns 2005-11-20 + 2005-11-25. On the first descent the sampling sequence aborted; Hayabusa came down softly, bounced and rested on the surface for about 30 minutes. The second touchdown was planned but the sample-collection projectile failed to fire on command. Both surface contacts kicked up regolith into the collection horn anyway. The team would not know whether material had been captured until the capsule's recovery 5 years later.

Late 2005. After the second touchdown, a hydrazine leak caused attitude loss and battery depletion. Two of its three reaction wheels had already failed; communications lost for 7 weeks. Earth-return window slipped by 3 years. Engineers eventually re-established contact and devised a recovery plan.

2008-2010. One ion engine assembled from the surviving halves of two damaged engines (neutralizer of one + ion source of another), powering Hayabusa back to Earth for sample return. Mission engineers became national heroes in Japan.

2010-06-13. Sample-return capsule splashed down at Woomera, Australia. The spacecraft itself burned in the atmosphere immediately afterward — the recovery imagery of the capsule descending under parachute while the spacecraft streaked overhead was widely shared. Capsule recovery returned ~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust (sub-milligram total) — the first asteroid sample ever returned to Earth. Confirmed Itokawa's S-type composition and rubble-pile structure.
First asteroid sample ever returned to Earth (~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust, sub-milligram total)

JAXA's Hayabusa (Japanese for 'falcon') flew the most heroic mission-save in spaceflight history. Launched 2003-05-09 on an M-V-5 with four μ10 ion thrusters — the first microwave-discharge ion engines ever flown. Arrived at 25143 Itokawa 2005-09-12 — a 540×270×210-m rubble-pile near-Earth asteroid. Two touchdowns (2005-11-20 + 25), both with sample-collection projectile failures, though regolith was kicked into the collection horn anyway. Then a hydrazine leak crippled attitude control, two of its three reaction wheels failed, communications lost for seven weeks, the Earth-return window slipped by three years. Engineers assembled a single working ion engine from the surviving halves of two damaged engines and nursed Hayabusa back to Earth. Sample capsule recovered at Woomera AUS 2010-06-13 returned ~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust (sub-milligram total) — confirming the asteroid's S-type composition and rubble-pile structure, and proving that asteroid sample return was possible.
